text: A sweep's method field picks one of three search strategies, and the choice matters as much as the search space itself. Grid, random, and Bayesian search make very different tradeoffs between coverage, sample efficiency, and parallelism.

Grid search is exhaustive but scales catastrophically with dimensionality. Random search, which samples each parameter independently, outperforms grid search at an equal budget whenever only a few hyperparameters actually matter — the common case. Bayesian search is the most sample-efficient of the three, building a probabilistic model of the metric surface to choose the next most informative trial, but it's inherently sequential.

A grid over three values each for two parameters is nine runs, guaranteed — add a third three-valued parameter and it's twenty-seven. Grid search wastes budget on fine-grained coverage of dimensions that might barely matter, which is exactly what makes it scale so badly.

Bayesian search builds a Gaussian-process-style model of how the metric depends on the hyperparameters and picks each next configuration to balance exploring the unknown against exploiting what already looks promising. That makes it dramatically more efficient per trial when training runs are expensive — but each suggestion depends on the last, so it parallelizes far worse than random or grid search.

Grid for small, exhaustive spaces; random when you've got many parallel workers; Bayesian when individual runs are expensive and parallelism is limited. Next: experiment tracking infrastructure — what a tracking backend actually needs to store as a sweep scales to hundreds of runs.
